The shared softmax denominator makes shallow-depth weights potentially depend on long context. Writing α_d=exp(a_d)/Σ_j exp(a_j), direct differentiation gives ∂α_d/∂x_s=α_d[∂a_d/∂x_s−Σ_j α_j∂a_j/∂x_s]. For an old input x_s outside shallow depth d’s receptive field, ∂a_d/∂x_s=0, yet deeper logits can depend on x_s and change α_d through normalization. Thus the shallow representation can remain local while its contribution is context-dependent. A large shallow weight indicates relative depth preference, not historical-context exclusion; deeper representations can also retain influence through their weighted values. This distinction aligns with evidence that attention weights alone need not explain prediction dependence. [Jain and Wallace, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10186).

Distinguish these mechanisms using computational receptive-field tracing, lag-wise Jacobians of representations, logits, gates and final scores, and paired history interventions that preserve recent events while replacing or truncating older events. Compare full recomputation against (1) fixed original gates with recomputed representations, isolating the value pathway, and (2) fixed original representations with recomputed gates, isolating the routing pathway. These are controlled internal interventions, not necessarily additive causal contributions; measure their interaction too. Fixed shallow-only readout tests exclusion only when its entire upstream computation has a bounded local receptive field. Detaching gradients through deeper logits does not remove their forward dependence on history. Report score/rank changes and validation effects across plausible history perturbations; zero local gradients or unchanged top-k results alone cannot establish exclusion. These proposed analyses follow the broader recommendation to test explanatory claims through interventions rather than weight inspection. [Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04626).
